newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Worried pet owners turn to animal psychics.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Worried pet owners turn to animal psychics.

text.p: When her dog's incessant barking started to get on her nerves, Cynthia Sloan knew where to turn for help. She went to an animal telepath.

While still a rare breed, animal psychics are increasingly in demand by doting pet owners who want to know what is on the minds of their dogs, cats and even birds and fish. The psychics claim to have a gift for communicating with animals and several in California have given up more mainstream careers to go into business as telepaths.

Pet owners most often go to animal telepaths to seek the cause of behavioural problems such as carpet-wetting or for help in deciding whether to "put their sick pets to sleep," telepaths say. Other owners want help in finding lost animals, or sometimes they just want to know what their pet thinks of their new girlfriend or boyfriend.

In Sloan's case, the problem was the barking habit of her 2-year-old Swiss cattle dog. Sloan brought the unruly dog, Hobie, to animal telepath Raphaela Pope's house in Berkeley. After investigating the house and meeting Pope's dog, cat, six birds, two rabbits and her husband, Hobie settled down in a cluttered living room for the psychic reading.
IS BARKING AN INHERITED CHARACTERISTIC IN DOGS?

As the dog relaxed, Sloan told Pope of her suspicion that Hobie inherited his yapping habit from his cow-herding ancestors. "I try to tell him he doesn't need to do that when we're playing with him or other dogs because they're not cows. Why does he need to bark so much when we play?" Sloan asked. "Is he getting it that we want him to be quiet?"
Pope closed her eyes and a look of concentration filled her face. She did not speak to the black, white and brown dog, which lay on the floor twitching, seemingly oblivious to the people around him.

After a short time Pope chuckled, opened her eyes and said Hobie was well aware of his owner's wish that he make less noise. "What he shows me is he reaches a pitch of excitement and he just can't not bark," Pope said.

She said she had asked Hobie to try to bark a little less and the dog replied that he would try to tone it down a little -- but that his owner would probably be better off not getting him excited in the first place.

The three-way conversation including Pope, Sloan and Hobie lasted for about half an hour, covering topics ranging from favourite games and toys to the dog's dreams and aspirations. Sloan left pleased and Hobie seemed a little more sedate.

Pope makes her living doing about 25 such consultations a week at a rate of $40 per half-hour session. Business is going so well she quit her part-time nursing job in October to focus exclusively on her career as a sort of animal interpreter.
DIDN"T WANT TO BE THOUGHT A LOONY
Pope, 53, says she has been communicating with animals for more than 20 years, but fear of jeopardising her nursing job kept her from capitalising on her talent until recently.

"I didn't want to be thought of as loony and I only did readings for friends and family and I kept very quiet about it. But a few years ago I got much more serious about it," she said with a smile. "I began to advertise judiciously and to tell friends and family to spread the word around."

Pope recalls helping a panicked woman who called from Arcata, some 250 miles (400 km) away, to find her lost cat, Bobby Kitty. Pope says she contacted the cat and had her describe her surroundings, then relayed the picture of boarded-up buildings and parking meters to the owner.
Sure enough, when the owner found the only place matching that description in the small town, Bobby Kitty was there.

Pope says she knows of only a handful of full-time animal telepaths and it is not a widely-known profession, so part of her advertising is teaching frequent workshops training others to communicate directly with their animals.
TALKING TO ANIMALS EASY IF YOU KNOW HOW
Sam Louie, another full-time telepath living in Berkeley, says most people are capable of communicating with animals if they can just let go of their scepticism.

"This is something everyone is born with. I believe this is something we lose along the way by developing such an emphasis on speech," Louie said. The Columbia Law School graduate has taught workshops with Pope and they often consult each other on particularly tough cases.
He says animal telepathy is not a highly lucrative field, but he has no second thoughts about quitting his steady job as a public defender a year ago to pursue telepathy as a career.

Lee Zasloff, associate director of the Centre for Animals in Society at the veterinary school of the University of California at Davis, admits to some scepticism about the possibility of telepathic communication between species.
"But I would not just discount it out of hand -- nobody knows about these kinds of things," she said.
